papers.tldr: CrysLDMは、3D結晶材料生成のための新しい潜在拡散モデルであり、変分オートエンコーダと拡散モデルを統合することで、効率的に安定した結晶材料を生成することを目指しています。従来のモデルよりも計算資源と時間を大幅に節約しつつ、最先端の手法と同等の品質を実現しています。

papers.title: DeclareViT: Decoupling Early Classification from Feature Refinement with Exit Query for Efficient ViTs
papers.summary: Vision Transformers achieve remarkable recognition performance but incur substantial computational cost during inference, limiting their use in latency- and compute-constrained deployment scenarios. Early-exit inference offers a promising solution by allowing easy samples to terminate at intermediate layers. However, existing approaches typically couple early classification with the shared backbone, requiring intermediate representations to support both early classification and subsequent feature refinement. Under joint training, the corresponding optimization objectives jointly update shared backbone parameters, which can lead to conflicting gradient directions. Motivated by this observation, we introduce DeclareViT, a framework that decouples early classification from feature refinement. Each exit uses a dedicated query to read intermediate features through one-way cross-attention without modifying the backbone token stream. The query branches are optimized for early classification while the backbone and final classifier remain frozen. Across ViT, DeiT, and Swin on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and Food-101, DeclareViT consistently establishes a state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off: It achieves 1.58 times to 2.57 times multiply-accumulate (MAC)-based speed-up with only a 0.39-1.91 percentage-point accuracy drop. Wall-clock measurements on CPU and GPU further demonstrate practical inference acceleration. Code is available at https://github.com/TUDa-HWAI/DeclareViT.
papers.tldr: DeclareViTは、早期分類を特徴の洗練から切り離すことで、効率的なVision Transformersを実現するフレームワークであり、CIFAR-100やImageNet-1Kなどのデータセットで、従来の手法に比べて1.58倍から2.57倍の速度向上を達成しつつ、精度の低下を最小限に抑えています。

papers.title: PROPS: Can Visual Generators Keep the Current Look of a Prop?
papers.summary: Many generation tasks draw the next image from a visual history, such as storyboards, illustrated stories and multi-turn editing. A new request often states what happens next without restating how earlier objects look. Instead of recovering an object's current look from the history, generators often redraw it from the request alone or bring back an outdated look, and the error can carry into later steps. We call this failure prop drift. Existing evaluations rarely isolate it, because similarity to the history rewards copying and a judge that sees a single history cannot tell a look recovered from that history from one the generator happens to prefer. We introduce PROPS, a benchmark of 2,257 pairs of twin histories that end on the same request but show one prop in two different looks. A pair passes only if the generator draws the matching look on each side and carries out the request, so a look preferred by the generator or the judge passes at most one side. All 34 open and closed systems we test show prop drift, and even systems that carry out the requested action on most sides often lose the current look of the prop. Swapping the planners and editors of agents further shows that both history understanding and image generation limit agent performance. We also build PROPS-Train, 80,250 training chains in four tracks whose targets recover an earlier state or carry scripted changes forward, and fine-tuning on it clearly improves all four tested models. Both datasets will be publicly released.
papers.tldr: TL;DR: PROPSは、視覚生成タスクにおける「プロップドリフト」を評価するためのベンチマークで、異なる外観のプロップを持つ双子の歴史ペアを用いて、生成モデルの性能を測定します。全てのテストしたシステムはプロップドリフトを示し、提案されたアクションを実行しても現在のプロップの外観を失うことが多いことが分かりました。

papers.title: Position-Skipped Distillation of Sparse-Attention Indexers: Train Short, Serve Long
papers.summary: Top-k sparse attention relies on an indexer, a lightweight per-layer module that ranks cached tokens so attention covers only the k highest-scoring ones. Indexers are usually distilled from dense attention at the full serving length, so every training step pays for long-context dense attention. We show that when an indexer is distilled on short sequences, its failure to generalise to longer contexts is driven mainly by rotary positional encoding (RoPE), not by degraded content matching. We propose position-skipped distillation: the indexer and the frozen teacher see short sequences whose position IDs contain a randomly placed gap, so neither ever processes more than the short training length. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, an indexer distilled on 8K tokens this way matches a 32K-distilled indexer to within about 0.5 perplexity up to 32K, and on DeepSeek-V2-Lite matches a 64K-distilled indexer at 64K with roughly 6x less training compute per token. On Llama-3.1-8B it trails the stronger 32K run by 0.6 perplexity, and at 64K simple position compression is often as good, so the main gain is training cost rather than quality. We also quantise indexer keys to 3-4 bits without retraining and score them with a fused integer kernel: at 4 bits, perplexity changes by at most 0.05 and the scan is 1.6-2.2x faster than half precision. In a current serving engine, the indexer speeds up decoding only for long contexts with multiple concurrent streams.
